subject: arts-music
lesson_title: Concept model A: composition and visual hierarchy
essential_question: How can understanding artistic voice and advanced composition help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
learning_objectives: Build a clear mental model of composition and visual hierarchy through an explicit worked example, demonstration, text, or phenomenon.
Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of composition and visual hierarchy.
Check, revise, or improve work about composition and visual hierarchy using stated success criteria.
lesson_success_criteria: The learner completes the central task about composition and visual hierarchy.
The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer.
The learner checks or revises the work and can identify a next step.
materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool
task_brief: Day 2 of "Artistic Voice and Advanced Composition" (unit 1, grade 8) is a first concept model on composition and visual hierarchy. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 40–60 minutes. The unit is working toward: Develop a coherent visual series with an artist statement and process evidence. Today's work contributes to that by handling composition and visual hierarchy at the concept model a stage, against the unit's wider topics of personal artistic questions, composition and visual hierarchy, symbol metaphor and abstraction, and style studies without copying. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Study the first model work for composition and visual hierarchy closely before making anything of your own. Write what you notice in three passes: first what is literally there, then how it is put together, then what effect that has on a viewer or listener. Name the specific choice the maker used to create composition and visual hierarchy. Then reproduce that one element — not the whole work — in your own short study, and write one sentence on what was harder than it looked. Use only public-domain, openly licensed, or supplied model works, and cite whatever you studied. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about composition and visual hierarchy, and it belongs to "Artistic Voice and Advanced Composition", which also covers separate topics such as personal artistic questions. Close out with this check before you stop: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about composition and visual hierarchy; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. At grade 8 the bar is independent work that anticipates the obvious objection: name the case most likely to break your result, test it, and report what happened.
requirements: Meet this lesson's own success criteria: The learner completes the central task about composition and visual hierarchy., The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer., and The learner checks or revises the work and can identify a next step.
Address the lesson objective: Build a clear mental model of composition and visual hierarchy through an explicit worked example, demonstration, text, or phenomenon.
Produce the deliverable for a first concept model: Three-pass observation notes, the named maker's choice, one single-element study, and a citation for the model work.
Show the process, not only the result — a working log, draft, or annotated study.
Complete the critique criteria list in this package before submitting.
deliverable: Three-pass observation notes, the named maker's choice, one single-element study, and a citation for the model work.
critique_criteria: Observation is recorded in three distinct passes: literal content, construction, and effect.
The specific maker's choice that creates composition and visual hierarchy is named, not described in general praise.
One element — not the whole work — is reproduced as a short study, with a note on what proved harder than expected.
Every studied work is public domain, openly licensed, or supplied for this task, and is cited.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available and scores the same. Instead of performing, speaking, or recording, you may submit a written description of what you made or would make, a notated or diagrammed version, a labelled plan, or a written analysis covering the same criteria. Nothing in this task requires a working microphone, camera, or the ability to perform aloud.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: This task centres a visual element (composition and visual hierarchy). Provide tactile, raised-line, or high-relief equivalents, enlarged and high-contrast print, and a verbal description route. Never make colour discrimination alone carry a criterion — pair any colour judgement with value, label, or texture.

Any model, source, or artifact under study is supplied in an accessible parallel form: text alternative or transcript, described version, and a tactile or enlarged rendering where the original is visual. The learner is never required to perceive the source in one specific channel to analyse it.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, copyright, cultural context, and respectful representation.
Provide a non-performance or low-audience option when needed without lowering the academic target.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting composition and visual hierarchy.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for composition and visual hierarchy follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for composition and visual hierarchy, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for composition and visual hierarchy works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of composition and visual hierarchy, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking composition and visual hierarchy mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply composition and visual hierarchy under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on composition and visual hierarchy rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
